prompt: What is Tufte's lie factor?

choices.text: The number of false values printed on a chart
choices.why: A chart can have no false value and a lie factor of 25.

choices.text: The effect shown divided by the effect in the data
choices.why: Right. A faithful chart scores 1.

choices.text: How far the axis starts from zero, in percent
choices.why: The start matters, but the factor compares two effects.

choices.text: The share of ink that carries no data
choices.why: That is closer to the data-ink idea of lesson 17.

prompt: Sales rose 10%. On a bar chart with a cut axis, the second bar is 50% taller than the first. What is the lie factor?
Which of these may start its value axis above zero?

choices.text: A line chart of temperature
choices.why: Right. A line is read by position and slope.

choices.text: A bar chart of orders by region
choices.why: A bar is read by its length from zero.

choices.text: A stacked area chart of revenue over the year
choices.why: A filled area is read from its baseline.

choices.text: A column chart comparing two years of sales
choices.why: Columns are bars standing up.

prompt: A bar chart starts its axis at 65,000 and marks the gap with a broken-axis symbol. Is it fixed?

choices.text: Yes: the reader is told about the cut
choices.why: Being told does not change what the eye compares.

choices.text: Yes, as long as the ticks are labelled
choices.why: Labels were there in the misleading version too.

choices.text: Only if the chart is horizontal
choices.why: Orientation does not change length.

choices.text: No: the bars are still the wrong length
choices.why: Right. The symbol confesses the cut without undoing it.

prompt: Tufte's ___ factor compares the effect a graphic shows with the effect in the data.
On a chart with two vertical axes, what decides where the two lines cross?

choices.text: The month the two series became equal
choices.why: The series are on different scales; a crossing says nothing about equality.

choices.text: The faster-growing of the two series
choices.why: Growth rates are hidden by the ranges, not shown by the crossing.

choices.text: The order in which the lines were drawn
choices.why: Drawing order decides which is on top, not where they meet.

choices.text: The ranges somebody chose for the axes
choices.why: Right. Change one range and the crossing moves.

prompt: When is a second vertical axis harmless?

choices.text: When both axes are clearly labelled in colour
choices.why: Labels do not stop the ranges deciding the crossing.

choices.text: When the two series have similar sizes
choices.why: Then one axis would do.

choices.text: When it is the same quantity in another unit
choices.why: Right, like Celsius and Fahrenheit: one scale written twice.

choices.text: When the right axis starts at zero
choices.why: The left one can still be tuned against it.

prompt: Which of these show two series of different sizes honestly? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: Two stacked panels sharing the time axis
choices.why: Right. Each gets an honest scale of its own.

choices.text: Index both to 100 at a common start, on one axis
choices.why: Right. One scale that nobody chose.

choices.text: A second axis whose range is tuned until the lines meet
choices.why: That is the trick, not the fix.

choices.text: Both series as 3D ribbons on one plot
choices.why: Depth adds distortion and fixes nothing.

choices.text: A scatter plot of one against the other
choices.why: Right, when the question is whether they move together.

prompt: A circle's radius is doubled to show a value that doubled. How many times larger is its area?
North's orders grew 1.605 times. To draw that honestly with circles, by how many times should the radius grow? Answer to three decimal places.
A cube is drawn twice as tall, twice as wide and twice as deep to show a value that doubled. How much larger is its volume?

choices.text: Twice, as it should be
choices.why: Only one dimension should have grown, and even then volume reads poorly.

choices.text: Four times, like a circle's area
choices.why: That is two dimensions; a cube has three.

choices.text: Six times, one per face of the cube
choices.why: Faces do not add up that way.

choices.text: Eight times as large as before
choices.why: Right. Two cubed.

prompt: An icon chart shows orders with shopping bags. What keeps it honest?

choices.text: Grow one bag in height and width with the value
choices.why: Its area grows by the square.

choices.text: Draw the bags in 3D so they look real
choices.why: Depth adds a third distortion.

choices.text: Repeat one bag of a fixed size, many times
choices.why: Right. Bags are counted, not estimated.

choices.text: Give each region a bag of a different colour
choices.why: Colour does not fix the size problem.

prompt: Horta's orders fell 19.8% from December 2024 to January 2025. Why is a chart of just those two months misleading?

choices.text: The fall was really larger than 19.8%
choices.why: The number is right; the window is the problem.

choices.text: December is a seasonal peak in each year
choices.why: Right. Every December spikes and falls back.

choices.text: Two months are too many to compare at once
choices.why: Two is too few, not too many.

choices.text: The chart should have been a pie instead
choices.why: A pie would not show time at all.

prompt: For a seasonal business, which comparison is fair?

choices.text: January 2025 with December 2024
choices.why: That compares a dip with a peak.

choices.text: The best month with the worst month of the year
choices.why: That measures the season, not the business.

choices.text: December 2025 with December 2024
choices.why: Right. Like with like.

choices.text: December 2025 with the average month of 2024
choices.why: A peak against an average flatters the peak.

prompt: Southeast grew 14.6%. Order these bar charts from the smallest lie factor to the largest.
In a tilted 3D pie, why does a slice at the front look bigger than its share?

choices.text: Its side wall shows as well as its top
choices.why: Right. Only the front slices get that extra ink.

choices.text: The software rounds its share upwards
choices.why: The numbers are not changed; the drawing is.

choices.text: Front slices are always given the largest category
choices.why: Here the front slice was the second-smallest.

choices.text: Its colour is brighter than the others
choices.why: The effect is geometry, whatever the colours.

prompt: When is a third dimension worth drawing?

choices.text: Whenever the chart goes into a printed annual report
choices.why: On paper the reader cannot rotate it.

choices.text: Data with three dimensions, and a reader who turns it
choices.why: Right, as in an interactive scientific plot.

choices.text: When a pie has more than five slices
choices.why: More slices make a 3D pie worse.

choices.text: When the audience expects something modern
choices.why: Style is not a reason to distort sizes.

prompt: What goes wrong when a value is read off a 3D bar?

choices.text: It is unclear which edge to read
choices.why: Right. The top face sits above the front face.

choices.text: The bar no longer starts at zero
choices.why: Depth does not move the baseline.

choices.text: The colours of the faces are hard to tell apart
choices.why: The trouble is reading the height.

choices.text: The gridlines disappear behind the bars
choices.why: They may, but the edge is the real problem.

prompt: This chart has four of the problems from this lesson. Find each one.

labels.text: an axis that does not start at zero
a line read on the second scale

hint: Read the lowest number on the left axis.

prompt: Match each distortion to its fix.

pairs.left: a bar axis that starts at 65,000
two lines on two vertical scales
pairs.right: index both to 100 on one axis

prompt: Every number on a chart is correct and every axis is labelled. Can it still mislead?

choices.text: No, a labelled chart is honest by definition
choices.why: Every chart in this lesson was labelled.

choices.text: Only if it uses more than one colour
choices.why: Colour was not the cause of any of these.

choices.text: Yes, through the choices behind it
choices.why: Right: the baseline, the ranges, the window, the shape.

choices.text: Only when it is drawn in a spreadsheet
choices.why: Any tool can draw any of these.
